#4790. In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

“I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in New York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney.

Cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

“We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” says the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it

Cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” says Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s New White.

The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” says Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”

The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

To expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” says Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

With a view over the living room, Cooney says the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

The clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

“I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” says Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” says Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

#4789. These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

We’re often told that certain scent ingredients can cause sensitivity and irritation. The latest innovations aim to do the exact opposite, nurturing your outer layer with next-generation formulas.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two issues at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” says Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” says Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

It’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

But it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do says.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”

Dr. Queller says that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”

Deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she says the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

The latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence important cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study showed that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The new Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-new blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist

Salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum

Each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

So, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”

What is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”

Elise Minton Tabin is an award-winning beauty journalist, editor, and expert with more than 19 years of experience. She started her career in public relations before shifting to editorial. Elise rose the ranks at NewBeauty magazine from an editorial assistant to Executive Beauty Editor, overseeing and reporting on all things beauty, plastic surgery, anti-aging, health, and wellness.

A prolific content creator and trendspotter, Elise always knows what’s new, what works, and who’s the best to go to for treatments and procedures. She has been featured on Extra TV, WPTV, and WPLG, on satellite tours, and as a featured expert in Perricone MD infomercials. She is also a regular contributor to InStyle.com, The Zoe Report, Byrdie, Beauty Independent, O Oprah Daily, and more. She also runs the Gen Z skincare brand, TWiiSH, with her teenage daughter, Madysen.

Brian Underwood is beauty director at Women’s Health, where he oversees content strategy for the brand across all platforms, including digital, print, and social. Underwood previously served as beauty and wellness director at Oprah Daily and O, The Oprah Magazine. During his tenure leading beauty content for the Oprah brand at Hearst, stories Underwood commissioned were awarded the Skin Cancer Foundation Media Award and a Fragrance Award for Editorial Excellence (his second). He was the launch Beauty Director of Dr. Oz THE GOOD LIFE, and has held additional editorial positions at Fitness, Organic Style, Good Housekeeping, Life & Style Weekly, and Woman’s Day and has written for Self, Shape, Seventeen, Redbook, Cosmopolitan, and many more. Underwood previously served on the Skin Cancer Foundation’s gala committee and as partnerships director of the Trans Beauty Clinic, a New York-based charitable organization that provided beauty services and workshops to the city’s trans community.

#4787. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4786. Mauviel's Copper Cookware Is 25% Off For Black Friday

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more quickly and evenly.

That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

The copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear shows quickly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

The Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.

#4784. The Best Hoka Walking Shoes In 2026, Tested By Podiatrists and Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There are many perks of being a Women’s Health style writer, and testing comfortable sneakers for work ranks very high on the list. My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand launched in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), says podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City.

Hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

After testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review

Technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

The midsole is stiff yet flexible, while the cushioning is relatively low-key compared to its popular sibling, the Bondi 9. But, its slimness is an illusion. In fact, it’s just as supportive as most Hoka models and still offers a spring-like sensation after your foot hits the ground for a comfortable stride. This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

I wear the standard size and haven’t had any issues, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.

While our one complaint with the Mach 6 was its lack of traction, I thankfully found that the Mach 7 features a more durable rubber at the heel and a stickier rubber up front, which makes a noticeable difference in grip.

Thanks to its incredible support and cushioning, the Gaviota 6 keeps my feet pain-free even after miles of wear. The shoe is designed with Hoka’s signature H-frame, which is a firm, dense foam in the midsole that provides a stable base to really lock your feet in place. I recently discovered that I have high arches, causing my ankles to roll inward when I walk, so this shoe has been a game-changer for me and my recent foot woes.

While the Gaviota 6 is geared toward flat arches on paper, I’m currently contending with a bit of foot fatigue from my new 1-mile-per-day (at least!) running goal, and the Gaviota 6 has given my dogs the TLC they need. That’s likely due to the combo of plush cushioning and stability tech. After weeks in the Gaviota 6, my gait naturally shifted from a heel strike to a midfoot strike—exactly what Schaeffer recommends for pain-free walking.

Other super supportive sneakers I’ve tried tend to have a stiff midsole. Not so with this shoe. It has a hefty EVA foam for a plush feel, like I’m walking on marshmallows. Plus, I found this foam also does a bang-up job of absorbing impact from my strides. In other words, it’s super easy on my joints. Bonus points: its fabric doesn’t rub at all, even when I’m wearing thin socks, which is a must-have when I’m clocking hundreds of miles in it.Weighing in at under nine ounces, the Gaviota 6 actually sheds half an ounce from the already lightweight Gaviota 5. I love that it feels lighter than it looks, but it still has a bulky look that may not vibe with everyone. FWIW, I love the chunky aesthetic and wear it with hiking gear, wide-leg trousers, and even casual dresses.

Plantar fasciitis (that painful inflammation under your arch) demands serious support, and the Hoka Bondi 9 delivers. It’s the brand’s plushest model, with cushioning that feels soft yet springy like you’re walking on clouds.

“I’ve been struggling with plantar fasciitis after months of half-marathon training, and this shoe—along with daily leg stretches—got me through long-haul walks pain-free,” says Accardi. That’s thanks to the Bondi’s plush underfoot cushioning and generous stack height. Schaeffer also recommends this shoe to his clients with plantar fasciitis, and says it provides a nice mix of cushion and stability. I also supinate and found that the Bondi 9’s premium foam midsole keeps my feet in a neutral position.

Contributor Lily Wohlner is also a mega-fan of this shoe. She's logged 15 miles walking in it and even wore it to the office to see how it holds up during long days on her feet. The verdict? It's the most comfortable shoe she owns, and she can wear it all day long without an ounce of foot pain.

Compared to the last iteration, this pair looks less bulky and feels lighter, and our style team found that this streamlined aesthetic plays nicer with most casual fits. However, be aware the shoe runs a tad narrow. Ritchey says she doesn’t have particularly wide feet, but that the toe box is a bit too small. She walked over 17 miles in this shoe recently and started to blister slightly in her pinky toes.

“The Arahi 8 has become my absolute companion running and walking shoe ever since I started bouncing back from my stress fracture,” Accardi says. “My podiatrist said I needed something firm and supportive—too much squish and flex could cause my feet to roll and exacerbate my injury—and the Arahi delivered.” Don’t let the sturdy midsole fool you: It’s relatively comfy for a stability shoe, with just enough give to keep things feeling smooth. Compared to the Arahi 7, this version hugs the foot better and offers noticeably more bounce-back with every step. It’s got that sweet spot of stability and responsiveness.

Fitness editor Cori Ritchey is a huge fan of the shoe’s “well-balanced cushioning,” saying that it feels plush underfoot but didn’t affect her stability while walking long distances or running. She loves that the toe box on the Arahi 8 is a bit wider than the Bondi 9, giving her plenty of room to spread her toes. But, if you are into plush, cloud-like cushioning, you may want to stick with the Bondi’s. The Arahi doesn’t have that marshmallow-like softness—it’s much firmer.

One of its standout features is the integrated H-frame support system: Strategically placed firmer foam that wraps around the sides of your foot to guide your stride and keep your foot in a neutral position. You can definitely feel the structure working, but the payoff in stability is huge, especially if you’re recovering, need extra support, or just want something you can rely on to keep your form in check.

As someone who never reties her shoe laces (I always slip my sneakers on), the Hoka Transport originally caught my eye with its toggle lace system that eliminates the hassle of tying and untying.

It reminds me of my favorite Salomon XT-6 shoes and has a cool granola-girl vibe—which makes sense, since it is technically a hiking shoe. However, I will admit that while the Transport 2 looks very similar to the original, I prefer the sleeker look of the previous iteration. This version is also slightly heavier, but it’s barely noticeable while walking, and I chalk it up to the slight increase in cushioning.

This shoe has quite a bit of cushion, but I found the midsole to be a bit on the stiffer side, meaning you just might want to plan for a longer break-in period before wearing it on long walks right off the bat. On the flip side, the firmness makes for a stable stride. It’s also great for neutral arches since it's not designed with any specific stability features in mind. But even with my slightly high arches, I felt locked in with every step.

Thanks to the high-traction, chunky outsole, I feel stable during trail walks across gravel, sandy paths, and uneven terrain. I also like that the outer shell material is Cordura, a water and abrasion-resistant mesh that’s built to prevent scuffs and withstand wear and tear.

One thing to note: I went with the standard width, and the fit is a bit snug, especially with thicker socks. If you have wider feet, consider sizing up or opting for the wide version.

Hoka is known for its incredibly cushioned sneakers, but extreme cushioning is not always the best for keeping feet stable. In recent years, Hoka has leveled up their offering with more stability options, but the right pick depends on how your foot moves. If your stride is balanced, go for a neutral shoe like the Clifton or Bondi. These models provide cushioning and support without changing your natural gait.

If your foot tends to roll inward (aka overpronation) or outwards (supination), a stability Hoka shoe like the Arahi or Gaviota features extra structure along the arch and heel to keep your feet aligned and locked in. This lowers your risk of aches and injury.

A popular Hoka sneaker, like the Bondi or Clifton, has super-thick cushioning made of EVA foam that is rubber-like and incredibly durable. With each step, it compresses and provides a snappy bounce. Despite the Hokas’ bulky look, they’re all relatively lightweight at under 10 ounces—hefty enough to keep your foot locked in, but light enough not to bog you down. Plus, several Hoka styles feature a "rocker bottom," which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to the base of a rocking chair. That shape helps you to walk from heel to toe, which means you exert less energy to propel your strides.

Some Hoka sneakers are designed for specific arch types: flat, neutral, and high. For example, the Gaviota is designed with flat feet in mind; the Clifton is designed for neutral arches; and the Bondi is suitable for high arches. If you’re unsure of your arch type, a simple test is to dip your foot into water and step onto a piece of paper. If you see your entire foot, it’s flat, while seeing half means it’s neutral. Seeing barely anything means you have a high arch.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

With their cloud-like cushioning, springy soles, and ample support, Hoka sneakers absorb impact from every step and keep feet locked in a neutral position. That makes them ideal for hot girl walks, a 12-3-30 walking workout, and taking your pup for a leisurely stroll.

Topping the list is the Hoka Clifton 11. I love the super supportive, plush midsole that keeps my feet from rolling and feels ultra-flexible. A close second is the Hoka Mach 7, our runner-up that’s technically a running shoe but totally crushes it for walking, too. It’s light, bouncy, and built for those who like to switch up their stride

Over the past two years, I’ve been testing Hoka sneakers alongside my team for a comprehensive approach to the best walking shoes for every foot type and stride. Women’s Health editors have been testing Hoka sneakers since the brand launched in 2009. For this update, I tested the updated models alongside WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey and fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi. Along with Schaeffer’s insights, I evaluated each for its cushioning, stability, and arch type.

#4782. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4779. 15 Best Places to Buy Bedding, Editor Picks (2026)

Sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

For bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she says. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”

Made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” says Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

Anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

Of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”

Boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she says. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

Brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

“Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” says AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”

Few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

“I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” says Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”

Shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

Cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” says contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”

Parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

“We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” says Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”

Fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she says.

GreenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”

Rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she says. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

Hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

Baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

Australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she says.

Erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

It depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

Start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more quickly and break apart in the washer and dryer.

#4778. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4776. The 11 Best Deodorants for Women in 2026, Tested by a Beauty Editor

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both important, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an issue for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose says your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.)

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

When it comes to selecting the best overall deodorant for women, it's tough to find a winner that doesn't include aluminum.
